paragraphs: Multi-metric learning adapts the meaning of distance to different parts of a feature space. This can make even simple classifiers competitive because nearby relationships reflect local data structure. The difficulty is that the resulting distance measure is non-metric, which has obstructed principled extensions to regression and dimensionality reduction.

The paper proves that, after appropriate changes, learning these local metrics can be understood as learning a Riemannian manifold. This supplies a coherent geometric interpretation of the learned structure. It also provides a basis for defining operations needed to move beyond classification while respecting how distances vary across the space.

The authors give a practical algorithm for computing geodesics, together with algorithms for exponential and logarithmic maps. These tools let many algorithms originally formulated in Euclidean space use the learned geometry. The approach is illustrated through regression and dimensionality reduction involving predictions of human body measurements from shape data. The contribution combines a geometric foundation with computational tools that make that foundation usable.
neurips-2012-a-geometric-take-on-metric-.tldr: A geometric interpretation of local metric learning provides practical tools for extending it to regression and dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates an entire matrix from observations of only some entries. The paper proposes a convex estimation method that combines nuclear and Frobenius penalties. This combination is called a spectrum elastic net, and its calibration step addresses bias introduced by the Frobenius part of the penalty.

The algorithm repeatedly fills missing entries using its current estimate, then updates the matrix through a scaled, soft-thresholded singular value decomposition. These two operations alternate until the matrix converges. Calibration follows this iterative fitting process. The procedure therefore separates obtaining a regularized estimate from correcting the particular bias caused by one of its penalties.

Under appropriate coherence conditions and suitable penalty levels, the authors prove an error bound with nearly optimal order that scales with the noise level. Those conditions are part of the guarantee. The same analysis covers both noisy observations and the noiseless case, providing a unified account of the estimator’s behavior. Simulations compare the proposal with earlier methods, although the abstract does not claim a particular empirical ranking.
neurips-2012-calibrated-elastic-regulari.tldr: A calibrated combination of matrix penalties yields nearly optimal, noise-proportional recovery guarantees under stated structural and tuning conditions.

paragraphs: Distributing statistical estimation across machines raises a practical question: how much accuracy can be retained with little communication? The paper studies two approaches that combine work performed on separate portions of a large dataset. Its analysis makes explicit how the number of machines interacts with the total amount of data.

The first method divides N samples evenly among m machines, minimizes an objective separately on each subset, and averages the resulting estimates. Under the stated conditions, its mean-squared error has order N⁻¹ + (N/m)⁻². When m is no larger than √N, this matches the best rate available to a centralized method using all samples.

The second method uses a suitable bootstrap construction and requires only one communication round. Its error has order N⁻¹ + (N/m)⁻³, making its guarantee more tolerant of increasing parallelization. The comparison shows why simply averaging local estimates can work well, and how the bootstrap method improves the dependence on local sample size. Experiments use large-scale problems from the Microsoft Learning to Rank dataset.
neurips-2012-communication-efficient-alg.tldr: Local averaging and a bootstrap-based alternative offer distributed estimation guarantees that quantify the accuracy cost of parallelization.

paragraphs: Comparing two probability distributions can require estimating where their densities differ and by how much. One approach estimates each density separately and then subtracts the estimates. The paper explains why this can work poorly: each estimation stage ignores the eventual subtraction, and relatively small errors in the individual estimates can produce a large error in the difference.

The proposed method estimates the density difference directly in a single procedure. Its fitting target is therefore the quantity needed for comparison, rather than two intermediate quantities. The authors derive a nonparametric error bound for a finite sample and show that the estimator attains the optimal convergence rate in their analysis.

The paper also connects the estimate to approximation of L2 distance between distributions. Experiments demonstrate its usefulness for robust distribution comparison, including class-prior estimation and change-point detection. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support treating density difference as an estimation problem in its own right, especially when the downstream task depends on differences rather than on recovering each density separately.
neurips-2012-density-difference-estimati.tldr: Directly estimating a density difference achieves an optimal convergence rate and supports practical distribution-comparison tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian models of perception combine a prior distribution with a likelihood function, but these two ingredients can otherwise be chosen with considerable freedom. The paper argues that the neural representation of sensory information supplies a constraint on both. In particular, efficient coding links them through the distribution of stimuli the system represents.

This connection changes what kinds of perceptual bias the model can produce. Its Bayesian estimates can move away from peaks of the prior, even though Bayesian estimation is often associated with attraction toward more probable values. Such repulsion is a possible consequence of the linked prior and likelihood, rather than evidence that the estimates necessarily abandon Bayesian inference.

The framework accounts for previously reported repulsive biases in visual orientation perception. Its predicted neuronal tuning characteristics also match reported orientation tuning properties in primary visual cortex. These findings connect a behavioral pattern with properties of the sensory representation within one account. The authors present efficient coding as a promising constraint on perceptual Bayesian models, rather than establishing it as the only explanation.
neurips-2012-efficient-coding-provides-a.tldr: Efficient sensory coding links Bayesian priors and likelihoods and can explain repulsive biases in visual orientation perception.

paragraphs: Complex time series call for flexible models of the hidden processes that produce observations. The paper develops inference for Gaussian process dynamical systems, a model class proposed for this purpose. Its focus is how to estimate the latent structure accurately enough to support useful predictions from rich sequential data.

The authors formulate approximate inference as message passing based on expectation propagation. Within this formulation, forward-backward smoothing is repeated, allowing information to pass through the sequence across multiple iterations. The central change is to place smoothing inside a general iterative framework, rather than treating an existing smoothing procedure as the complete inference method.

The resulting posterior distributions over latent structures are reported to be more accurate, with better predictive performance than leading GPDS smoothers considered in the paper. Those smoothers are also special cases of the proposed algorithm. The contribution therefore has two connected roles: it improves inference through iteration and supplies a common framework for understanding how existing GPDS message-passing methods relate to one another.
neurips-2012-expectation-propagation-in-.tldr: An iterative expectation-propagation framework unifies GP dynamical-system smoothers and improves reported latent-state inference and prediction.

paragraphs: The paper addresses inference for Gaussian processes whose likelihood functions are non-conjugate. The supported settings include binary classification, multiclass classification, and ordinal regression. These tasks motivate an inference procedure that can handle the likelihoods used for their outputs while retaining the Gaussian process modeling framework.

The proposed solution is a variational inference algorithm built around a convex lower bound. Instead of directly carrying out the original inference calculation, the method optimizes this bound using efficient fixed-point updates. The bound and update procedure are the central computational contributions: together they provide a tractable optimization route for the non-conjugate cases covered by the method.

The authors report that the approach is much faster than existing methods in their empirical comparisons, with no degradation in performance. This is an experimental finding about the evaluated settings, rather than a universal speed guarantee. Its practical significance is that the reported computational savings do not require sacrificing the measured predictive performance, making inference efficiency the principal benefit highlighted by the paper.
neurips-2012-fast-bayesian-inference-for.tldr: A convex-bound variational algorithm speeds up non-conjugate Gaussian process inference without performance loss in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic optimization when an algorithm receives noisy function values but no gradients. Its central question is how quickly such methods can converge with a finite number of observations. This directly measures the price of using value information in place of the directional information supplied by a gradient.

When pairs of function values are available, the authors analyze algorithms that estimate gradients through random perturbations. They show that the convergence-rate penalty relative to traditional stochastic gradient methods is at most the square root of the problem dimension. The availability of paired values is a condition of this comparison and matters when interpreting the result.

The analysis also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on minimax convergence rates. These show that the algorithmic bounds are sharp in all problem-dependent quantities, up to constant factors. Thus, within the studied setting, the dimension-dependent cost is supported by both an achievable method and a matching fundamental limit. The result explains how much can be recovered from noisy value queries and where further rate improvements are ruled out.
neurips-2012-finite-sample-convergence-r.tldr: With paired noisy function values, random-perturbation methods achieve sharp convergence bounds with at most a square-root dimension penalty.

paragraphs: Finding an exact maximum a posteriori assignment is intractable in many practical problems, motivating linear-programming relaxations. Efficient solvers for these relaxations often use block coordinate descent. However, such methods can stop at suboptimal points, so their computational speed alone does not ensure that they solve the relaxed optimization problem globally.

The paper augments these algorithms with an epsilon-descent approach. It uses a margin-based extension of Fenchel–Young duality to efficiently find a descent direction within the subdifferential. This supplies a mechanism for making progress beyond points where the original coordinate procedure can become stuck, addressing the lack of global convergence.

The framework also provides a way to construct an optimal primal solution from an optimal dual solution. That links solving the dual optimization problem to recovering a solution of the original relaxation. Experiments on spin glass models and protein interaction problems report better performance than leading solvers. The global optimization target here is the MAP linear-programming relaxation; the abstract does not equate solving it with exact MAP inference in every problem.
neurips-2012-globally-convergent-dual-ma.tldr: A Fenchel–Young margin-based descent mechanism gives MAP LP relaxation solvers global convergence and a route from dual to primal solutions.

paragraphs: Sparse inverse covariance estimation is an important problem in graphical modeling, especially when selecting models in high dimensions. Many approaches use convex objectives with an l1 penalty. The paper focuses on a computational question that remained insufficiently resolved: how quickly an optimization method approaches the solution of this penalized estimation problem.

The authors propose an iterative thresholding algorithm based on proximal gradients for the l1-penalized maximum likelihood objective. They prove that it converges at a linear rate. Here, linear convergence describes the optimization rate across iterations, rather than saying that runtime grows linearly with the number of variables.

The convergence rate is given explicitly and depends on the condition number at the optimum. This connects a property of the solution to the predicted speed of the numerical method. The authors identify the result as the first linear-rate guarantee of its kind for this estimation problem and provide numerical results demonstrating the proven behavior. The contribution strengthens understanding of the solver’s convergence, rather than claiming that every aspect of statistical model selection is optimal.
neurips-2012-iterative-thresholding-algo.tldr: An iterative thresholding solver for sparse inverse covariance estimation has a proven linear convergence rate tied to the optimum’s conditioning.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks are deep models assembled from sum and product nodes. Although they had shown competitive performance on tasks such as image completion, choosing a suitable network architecture remained an open problem. This paper addresses that design decision by learning the architecture from the data.

The key step is to cluster variables according to their interactions. Grouping variables identifies subsets whose relationships deserve to be represented together. The algorithm then allocates network nodes toward explaining those interactions. Architecture selection is therefore guided by relationships within the modeled data, giving the network a structure tailored to the dependencies the learning procedure discovers.

Experiments show a significant performance improvement over a previously proposed static architecture. This supports the value of learning the network’s organization in addition to using the sum-product modeling framework itself. The reported comparison concerns the learned architecture and that static alternative; it does not establish superiority over every deep model. The main contribution is a concrete, data-driven strategy for deciding where an SPN should devote its representational structure.
neurips-2012-learning-the-architecture-o.tldr: Clustering interacting variables guides sum-product network architecture learning and improves performance over a fixed architecture in experiments.

paragraphs: An image’s overall memorability can be estimated from visual features, but that leaves a more local question: which parts of the image are likely to be forgotten? The paper moves from predicting a single property of an entire image toward modeling how memory relates to its individual regions.

The authors propose a probabilistic, data-driven framework that combines local information with features of the image as a whole. It models which regions may be forgotten and automatically produces memorability maps for individual images without human annotation. These maps express regional differences while allowing the surrounding image to contribute to the prediction.

The algorithm incorporates multiple attributes of image regions, and the resulting model improves overall image memorability prediction relative to previous work. This connects the regional analysis to a measurable benefit for the broader prediction task. The findings suggest that local and global image information together help explain memorability, while the probabilistic formulation preserves the distinction between a predicted tendency to forget a region and a certain outcome for every viewer.
neurips-2012-memorability-of-image-regio.tldr: A probabilistic model learns regional memorability maps from local and global image features and improves overall memorability prediction.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification predicts several labels for each example. A compressed-sensing approach first projects the label vector into a smaller space and then learns regression functions for those projections. The paper brings these two components into one Bayesian model, allowing compression and prediction to be optimized jointly.

The authors derive an efficient variational inference procedure that provides a joint posterior distribution over unobserved labels. This probabilistic treatment supports datasets with missing labels and supplies uncertainty estimates for predictions. Missing information therefore becomes part of the inference problem, while uncertainty provides more than a single proposed label assignment.

The uncertainty estimates also support active learning: an oracle can be asked about labels expected to be especially informative for prediction. Experiments report significant predictive improvements over prior methods on benchmark datasets with both complete and incomplete labels. The paper further describes active-learning scenarios enabled by the model. Its contribution is thus a unified treatment of label compression, missing-label inference, and uncertainty-guided requests for additional label information.
neurips-2012-multilabel-classification-u.tldr: A joint Bayesian model of label compression and prediction handles missing labels, estimates uncertainty, and enables active learning.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture models learned directly from natural image patch pixels had shown unexpectedly strong performance. This paper investigates both how well this relatively simple model works and what it learns. The authors report that it competes with highly successful image models on likelihood scores, denoising, and the quality of generated samples.

The analysis examines how learned properties change with the number of mixture components. It considers covariance structure and contrast variation, as well as more intricate visual patterns such as textures and boundaries. This makes the investigation about the model’s representation of image structure, alongside its performance on evaluation tasks.

The paper then connects those learned properties to a simplified Dead Leaves model, which explicitly represents occlusion. Salient characteristics of the image-trained Gaussian mixture can be derived from this model. That connection offers an explanation for why a mixture learned from pixels can capture important natural-image regularities: its learned statistics are related to a model of objects obscuring one another. The result provides an account of its success beyond simply observing strong scores.
neurips-2012-natural-images-gaussian-mix.tldr: An analysis of strong Gaussian mixture image models links their learned properties to an occlusion-based Dead Leaves model.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression with multiple response variables and a shared set of predictors. It extends reduced-rank regression beyond linear models by estimating an additive model for each response dimension. The goal is to retain flexibility in the individual prediction functions while controlling the complexity of the collection as a whole.

To impose that control, the authors introduce a functional version of the Ky-Fan, or nuclear, norm. This produces a collection of estimated functions with low rank. The rank restriction applies across the function estimates, bringing the organizing idea of reduced-rank linear regression into a nonparametric setting.

The paper derives backfitting algorithms and justifies them using a nonparametric nuclear-norm subdifferential. It also establishes oracle inequalities for excess risk that describe how the procedure scales in high dimensions. These results address both how to compute the estimates and how their predictive risk behaves in the analysis. An application to gene expression data illustrates the methods, connecting the multivariate formulation to a setting with multiple quantities to predict.
neurips-2012-nonparametric-reduced-rank-.tldr: A functional nuclear-norm penalty extends reduced-rank regression to multivariate additive models, with algorithms and high-dimensional risk guarantees.

paragraphs: Minwise hashing is useful for learning from massive binary datasets, but applying many permutations can make preprocessing expensive. The same cost arises at prediction time when a new document or image has not already been processed. The paper targets this repeated transformation work as an important obstacle to practical use.

The authors introduce a hashing scheme that uses one permutation. Its purpose is to reduce the work required before similarity estimation or learning can proceed. Although preprocessing can be parallelized, the abstract points out that doing so requires additional hardware and implementation effort. Reducing the number of permutations addresses the amount of work itself.

The paper develops a probability analysis and tests the method on similarity estimation, support vector machines, and logistic regression. The experiments confirm the theoretical results. The authors also argue that replacing many permutations with one would be more energy-efficient, a potentially relevant benefit in search applications. The abstract presents this energy consideration as motivation rather than reporting a measured energy saving.
neurips-2012-one-permutation-hashing-4f2.tldr: One-permutation hashing reduces the transformation work behind minwise hashing, with theoretical results supported by similarity and classification experiments.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to allocate samples when estimating a noisy function over a continuous space. The space is divided beforehand into finitely many cells, and each cell receives a constant approximation. The objective is to keep the local squared approximation error comparably low across all cells.

This extends an active-learning version of the multi-armed bandit problem, where the learner tries to estimate every arm’s mean with equal precision. Here, each arm corresponds to a region of the continuous sampling space. The shift matters because the task now concerns approximating a function within regions, rather than only estimating a finite collection of unrelated means.

The authors show that a simple upper-confidence-bound algorithm can adapt to the function in a near-optimal way. The guarantee requires the number of partition cells to have minimax-optimal order for the class of alpha-Hölder functions. Thus, the result combines adaptive sampling with a suitably sized partition fixed in advance. It supports confidence-based allocation for balancing regional errors under that smoothness-class and partition-size condition.
neurips-2012-online-allocation-and-homog.tldr: Upper-confidence-bound sampling nearly optimally balances local approximation errors when a fixed partition has a suitably chosen size.

paragraphs: The paper studies sum-product computation on a tree when data arrive continuously and individual results must be queried repeatedly. Computing a vertex’s marginal distribution in a tree-structured Markov random field is a motivating application. Standard belief propagation takes time linear in the tree size, making repeated online computations costly.

The proposed approach organizes the tree into a hierarchical covering structure and caches previous local sum-product calculations. This makes stored work available for later updates and marginal queries. The authors aim for operations taking no more than logarithmic time in tree size, with costs often substantially smaller.

The contribution includes a linear-time algorithm for finding an optimal hierarchical cover and a sum-product-style procedure that computes marginals using that cover. The paper also applies these tools to online allocation in a multitask setting, obtaining an efficient algorithm with a regret bound. The broader idea is that organizing and retaining intermediate computations can make a tree-based inference method better suited to a sequence of changing data and targeted queries.
neurips-2012-online-sum-product-computat.tldr: A hierarchical tree cover caches local sum-product work to support efficient online updates, marginal queries, and multitask allocation.

paragraphs: The paper asks what least-squares regression can gain by allowing a model to decline some predictions. This reject option produces a selective regressor: it predicts on part of the input domain and rejects elsewhere. The objective is to obtain stronger control over predictions where the model does choose to respond.

The authors show that rejection makes it theoretically possible to track, point by point within an epsilon tolerance, the best regressor in hindsight from the same hypothesis class. The rejected part of the domain has bounded volume. Under certain conditions, that volume tends to zero as the training set grows, so the theoretical benefit need not require permanently rejecting a fixed share of inputs.

For linear regression, the paper develops efficient, exact implementations of these selective regressors. Evaluation on real-world datasets supports the theoretical analysis and indicates substantial reductions in estimation error. The comparison target remains the best regressor within the chosen class. The result explains how selective prediction can trade coverage for more accurate estimation, with increasing data potentially reducing the amount of rejection required.
neurips-2012-pointwise-tracking-the-opti.tldr: Allowing regression to reject some inputs enables pointwise tracking guarantees and can reduce estimation error in practice.

paragraphs: Classification systems involving human intervention need decisions that people can inspect and understand. The paper approaches this through informative projections of the data, while seeking to make few assumptions about the underlying distribution. It formulates the task as finding axis-aligned subspaces, so the projections correspond to selections of existing feature dimensions.

The approach assumes that information specific to each query determines how different subspaces should complement one another. The proposed regression-based method, RECIP, finds projections by minimizing a nonparametric estimate of conditional entropy. This criterion directs the search toward projections that reduce uncertainty relevant to classification.

Experiments report that RECIP accurately identifies informative projections and selects suitable ones for classifying query points. The projections also facilitate visual evaluation by users. These findings connect predictive usefulness with inspectability: the selected views serve both the classification procedure and the person evaluating it. The query-specific assumption is central, because the method’s formulation allows different points to call for different informative views of the same dataset.
neurips-2012-projection-retrieval-for-cl.tldr: RECIP retrieves query-relevant feature projections that support accurate classification and visual inspection by users.

paragraphs: Derivative-free optimization is useful when derivatives are unavailable and function evaluations are costly. Noise makes estimating gradients from finite differences especially difficult. The paper establishes quantitative lower bounds showing a fundamental performance gap between access to noisy function values and access to noisy gradients in the setting it studies.

These bounds challenge the idea that finite differences can simply substitute for stochastic gradients at comparable cost. The authors also provide a new algorithm for situations where derivative-free optimization is unavoidable. It is proved near-optimal for strongly convex objectives and uses Boolean-valued comparisons between function values rather than requiring their numerical values.

Comparison-only feedback broadens the possible applications, including optimization driven by human paired comparisons. A further result is that noisy numerical evaluations and Boolean-valued comparisons have the same convergence rate in the paper’s analysis. Thus, richer numerical feedback does not improve that rate over comparisons in this setting. The contribution combines a limit on what derivative-free methods can achieve with an algorithm that approaches the limit using particularly simple feedback.
neurips-2012-query-complexity-of-derivat.tldr: The paper proves noisy derivative-free optimization limits and gives a near-optimal comparison-only algorithm for strongly convex objectives.

paragraphs: Maximizing expected return is a common approach to planning under uncertainty, but an average outcome may be an unsuitable objective when risk matters. The paper proposes a different optimization objective for risk-aware planning in Markov decision processes. Its purpose is to bring risk considerations directly into what the planner optimizes.

The authors establish desirable theoretical properties of the objective and connect it to several existing approaches: minmax planning, exponential utility, percentile objectives, and mean minus variance. These connections place the proposal within a broader set of ways to express risk preferences, helping relate its formulation to alternatives already used for uncertain decisions.

The method permits stochastic costs, provided those costs are bounded, and the paper supplies an efficient optimization algorithm. Boundedness is therefore a stated condition on the extended class of decision processes it handles. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate effectiveness at scale. Together, the results provide a risk-aware objective, a computational procedure for optimizing it, and experimental evidence of its practical use.
neurips-2012-risk-aversion-in-markov-dec.tldr: A new risk-aware planning objective comes with theoretical properties and an efficient algorithm for MDPs with bounded stochastic costs.

paragraphs: Feature selection for linear regression usually seeks a small set of useful predictors. This paper also asks that the selected features be diverse, motivated by interpretability and robustness to noise. The aim is to make diversity an explicit part of the selection objective while retaining predictive usefulness.

The authors propose several spectral regularizers that express a notion of feature diversity and prove that these regularizers are submodular set functions. Adding them to the regression objective yields approximately submodular objectives. This structure allows efficient greedy and local-search algorithms to seek approximate solutions with provable guarantees.

Comparisons with traditional greedy selection and l1 regularization show that the proposed algorithms select more diverse features and produce regression problems that remain stable under perturbations. The empirical finding therefore links the diversity criterion to the motivating robustness concern. The theoretical contribution explains why the combined objective can be optimized approximately with guarantees, while the experiments show how the resulting selections behave relative to the evaluated alternatives.
neurips-2012-selecting-diverse-features-.tldr: Spectral diversity penalties enable feature-selection algorithms with approximation guarantees and improved perturbation stability in experiments.

paragraphs: A linear representer theorem says that a regularized learning problem admits a minimizer in the finite-dimensional subspace spanned by the data’s representers. This property underlies regularization theory and kernel methods. It matters because the solution can be sought in a data-defined subspace even when the surrounding Hilbert space is much larger.

Earlier characterizations covered certain families with differentiable regularization terms. They linked the representer property for every possible dataset to penalties that are radial and nondecreasing: the penalty depends on distance from the origin and does not decrease as that distance grows. The paper weakens the assumptions needed for this characterization.

Its main result implies that, for a sufficiently large family of regularization functionals, radial nondecreasing penalties are the only lower semicontinuous regularization terms that guarantee a representer theorem for every dataset. The scope of the family and the requirement to cover all data choices are essential qualifications. The result extends the structural characterization beyond differentiable penalties and clarifies which penalty shapes can support this universal representer guarantee.
neurips-2012-the-representer-theorem-for.tldr: The paper extends representer-theorem characterizations to weaker regularity assumptions, identifying radial nondecreasing penalties as essential within its stated scope.

paragraphs: Memristive devices can represent plastic synapses because applied electrical waveforms change their resistance. Many implementations had focused on finding waveforms that produce spike-timing-dependent plasticity, without closely matching biological waveforms or addressing other forms of plasticity. This paper uses a biologically motivated model to guide the device behavior.

The authors adapt a neuron-waveform-driven plasticity model to BiFeO3 memristive material. The model had explained a broad range of experimental observations. With this adaptation, they demonstrate spike-timing-dependent plasticity in the material for the first time and report better replication of the learning window than previous memristor-based implementations.

Measurements also demonstrate that short-term and long-term plasticity can coexist in the device through triplet plasticity. This extends the demonstrated behavior beyond the timing-dependent learning window alone. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first physical memristive implementation of triplet plasticity. The contribution connects a biologically grounded waveform model to measured device behavior, showing that the hardware can express more than one relevant form of synaptic change.
neurips-2012-waveform-driven-plasticity-.tldr: A biologically motivated waveform model enables timing-dependent and triplet plasticity in BiFeO3 memristive devices.
